headline: Niantic Fleet Grinding Fluke at 35 Feet While Black Point Sea Bass Bail Out the Coolers
subhead: A cold pocket parked off New London has the drift boats adjusting on the fly, but structure fishing at Black Point and Hole-in-the-Wall is keeping the mates busy at the cleaning table.
body_markdown:
Ran into one of the Niantic charter guys at the bait shop Thursday morning loading up on spearing and squid strips, and the first thing out of his mouth was, "You believe this water?" He'd just come off a half-day trip and said the temp gauge was sitting in the mid-60s off the mouth of the river — which for the second week of July is flat-out weird. New London's reading 66.4 right now, and that's cold enough that it's basically running ten degrees behind what Kings Point and the western Sound are seeing. Whatever's pushing that cooler water in — could be an upwelling event off the Race, could just be a run of easterly wind stacking it up — it's got the fleet adjusting game plans on the fly instead of running the same drift they ran in June.

The fluke bite reflects it. Niantic Bay and the flats off Twotree Island Channel are still holding fish, but they're not as aggressive as you'd want for mid-summer. The boats that are scoring are working slower drifts in 30 to 40 feet, dragging four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid to give the bait something to chew on instead of just swat at. Bigger fish — a few in the 4 to 6 pound class — have come off the deeper edge of the channel on the last two hours of the outgoing, when the current's still got some push but isn't ripping. Slack water has been dead in there this week. If you're marking bait but not getting bit, don't sit on it — that cool water has the fluke sluggish and they need a little current to trigger them.

Black Point has been the more consistent producer, and it's sea bass, not fluke, doing the heavy lifting. Structure in 25 to 45 feet off the Point has been stacked with keeper-class bass, and the drift boats working there are putting solid numbers in the box on Gulp squid rigs and green crab baited high-low rigs bounced right on the rockpiles. The bite's been best on the front half of the incoming tide, before the current gets too strong to hold bottom without going up in weight. Hole-in-the-Wall is fishing the same way — it's classic sea bass water, current-scoured ledge and boulder, and with the water staying cooler than normal those fish haven't scattered off the structure the way they sometimes do once things get properly hot. That's actually working in our favor right now.

Porgies are the easy button this week if you've got kids or a slower afternoon planned. The mouth of the Niantic River and the inner bay have been thick with scup in the 8 to 10 inch range, some better ones mixed in, and they'll eat anything — squid, sandworms, clam strips on a simple two-hook bottom rig in 15 to 25 feet. Good confidence-builder bite, and it's been steady through both tide stages, which is more than I can say for most everything else out there right now.

Striper action has been a mixed bag — present, but you have to work for it. Bluefish showed up in decent numbers off McCook Point and along the beach toward Black Point earlier in the week, blitzing on peanut bunker schools right at first light, and a few schoolie stripers have been mixed in with them on topwater plugs and small metal — half-ounce Deadly Dicks and Ava jigs worked well when the blitzes were tight to the surface. But it's been an early-morning window only. By 8 or 9 a.m. the bait pushes off and the bite goes quiet. If you want a shot at the bigger bass, the report from the guys running bunker chunks off Twotree has been better after dark — a handful of fish in the 28 to 34 inch range coming on fresh bunker chunks fished on the bottom near the channel edge on the last of the ebb.

Blackfish season's open now inshore, and while it's early for the structure bite to really turn on, a few boats poking around Hatchett Reef and the rockier stretches off Black Point have picked at some smaller tog on green crab. Nothing to build a trip around yet — that pattern usually doesn't get serious until the water cools back down in September — but worth knowing it's legal and there are fish there if you want to scout early.

Looking ahead, I'd keep an eye on that New London temp reading. If it climbs back into the low 70s where it should be for July, I expect the fluke bite to turn more aggressive and the sea bass to spread off the tightest structure onto the open bottom, which usually means better numbers but a little more hunting to find them. If the cool water holds, stick with what's working — slow drifts on the fluke, tight to structure for the bass, and fish the tide stages that give you current without overpowering it. Either way, Black Point and Hole-in-the-Wall are the safer bets to fill a cooler this week, with the fluke grounds needing the right window to really produce.
